newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura trust banking unit seeks quality.
newsitem.headline: Nomura trust banking unit seeks quality.

text.p: Akira Kiyokawa is confident the trust banking arm of Nomura Securities Co Ltd will become the most profitable bank in the world on a per-employee basis.
"Within the next two years, we want to post the biggest profit per head of any bank in the world," Kiyokawa, president of Nomura Trust and Banking Co Ltd, said in an interview.

The bank started its banking and trust business operations three years ago following reforms of Japan's financial system that took effect in April 1993. The changes were aimed at boosting competition and efficiency by allowing brokerages and banks to operate on each other's turf.

Trust banking units were required by the Ministry of Finance (MOF) to operate in the black within three years of starting, and Nomura cleared the requirement in fiscal 1995/96, which ended on March 31.

In 1995/96, it reported 1.63 billion yen ($14.8 million) in current profit and 1.3 billion yen ($11.8 million) in net profit. The year before, it had posted a current loss of 60 million yen ($545,000) and a net loss of 58 million yen ($527,000).

Nomura Trust and Banking, capitalised at 30 billion yen ($272 million), started operations with an initial work force of 71. Now the number has risen to about 90, but Kiyokawa does not plan to raise it beyond 100.
"With the current range of business, I don't think we need to increase the number. My focus is on the amount of money and the quality of business we can handle with a small number of people.

"We are posting an estimated 20 million yen ($181,000) of net profit per person a year now. To match that performance, a bank with staff of 20,000 would need some 400 billion yen ($3.63 billion) in net profit," he said.
That is the size of the work force at the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd, born in April as the world's largest bank in terms of assets following a merger between Mitsubishi Bank and Bank of Tokyo.
The combined parent current profit of the Bank of Tokyo and Mitsubishi Bank was 226.5 billion yen ($2.05 billion) in 1995/96, and their net profit added up to 51.1 billion yen ($464 million).
Nomura Trust and Banking's main operations fall into three areas -- foreign exchange and money market, investment trust and trust business.
"I am not interested in ordinary lending business. We are not eligible to join the business," Kiyokawa said.
Banking industry sources said Nomura's foreign exchange operation was particularly notable.

The trust bank basically does not handle trade-related currency business, but instead makes its money by handling currency deals in relation to stock investments in Asia and emerging markets on behalf of Japanese institutional investors and securities houses, they said.
The recent volume of Nomura's currency transactions was comparable to that traditionally done by a medium-sized Japanese commercial bank, they said.

Kiyokawa said profits from foreign exchange business range from 50 million yen ($454,000) to 150 million yen ($1.36 million) a month, and annual transactions total about five trillion yen ($45.4 billion).
In the foreign exchange and money market division, there are five spot dealers, four customer dealers, two money traders and four swap and derivatives traders.
"Even Bank of Japan and other bank officials are surprised at our foreign exchange operations," Kiyokawa said.
"Even with only such a small number of people, we can do good business... It's because we are supported by the name of Nomura," he added. ($1=110 yen)
